The 2026 United States Senate elections were held on November 3, 2026, with 33 of the 100 seats in the Senate being contested in regular elections. In these elections, voters elected candidates to six-year terms that begin on January 3, 2027, and expire on January 3, 2033. The Senate Democratic Caucus is projected to have gained a majority of between 54 and 56 seats, which would be its largest majority after an election since 2012.[1]

Senators are divided into three classes whose terms are staggered, so that a different class is elected every two years. Class 2 senators were last elected in 2020. With the election of John Thune as leader of the Republican Conference, this was the first election year since 2006 in which Senate Republicans were not led by Mitch McConnell. The Senate Democratic Conference has been led by Chuck Schumer since 2017.

Special elections were also held in Ohio and Florida, following the resignation of JD Vance to become vice president and Marco Rubio's resignation to become United States secretary of state. The appointed incumbents in these races were Republicans Jon Husted and Ashley Moody, both of whom were running to complete their terms until 2028.

Two incumbent senators—Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and John Cornyn of Texas—lost renomination in their respective primaries, while two nominees—Graham Platner (who dropped out) and Lindsey Graham (who died)—were replaced by a convention in Maine and a special primary in South Carolina, respectively. In three states (Idaho, Nebraska, and South Dakota), the Democratic nominee withdrew from the race, effectively clearing the field for an independent candidate.

Democrats have won 20 out of 35 contested seats, including 7 Republican-held seats. Republicans have defended 13 seats. Two seats (Alaska and Mississippi) remain undecided as of November 9, 2026[update].

Partisan composition

All 33 Class 2 Senate seats and two Class 3 seats were up for election in 2026. Class 2 currently consists of 20 Republicans and 13 Democrats.[2] Democrats defended two seats in states won by Donald Trump in 2024, in both cases by less than 3 percentage points: Michigan, where incumbent Gary Peters did not run for reelection; and Georgia, where the incumbent is Jon Ossoff. Michigan elected Democrat Elissa Slotkin to the Senate in 2024 by 0.3 percentage points. Georgia did not have a Senate election in 2024, although in its most recent Senate election, in 2022, Democrat Raphael Warnock won by three points in a runoff.[3][4]

Five incumbent Democratic senators represent states won by Kamala Harris by single-digit margins in 2024: New Hampshire's Jeanne Shaheen, Minnesota's Tina Smith, Virginia's Mark Warner, New Jersey's Cory Booker, and New Mexico's Ben Ray Luján.[3] Shaheen and Smith did not run for reelection.[5] Susan Collins's seat in Maine was the only seat defended by a Republican in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024.[6] Republican Thom Tillis of North Carolina chose not to run for reelection[7] in a state that Trump won by a single-digit margin in 2024.[3]

The 2026 Senate map was considered favorable to Republicans, even though Democrats defended 13 seats and Republicans 22. Most rating groups identified two Republican-held seats as highly competitive and three or four others as somewhat competitive. By contrast, Democrats needed to flip at least four seats to win a majority while defending two highly vulnerable seats and two others viewed as somewhat vulnerable.[8][9][10] Pollsters found Democrats' chances to flip the Senate to be improving as the election approached due to highly competitive campaigns by nominees in states such as North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, and Alaska, and because of Donald Trump's unpopularity amid the 2026 Iran war.[11][12][13]

Defeats

Six Republicans (including two appointees) sought either reelection or election (either to finish the term or a full six-year term), but lost either in the primary election or a special/general election. The last elected incumbent senator to lose renomination was Richard Lugar in 2012,[n] and the last time multiple elected incumbent senators lost renomination in primaries was in 2010.[o] The last incumbent senator to place no better than third in a primary before Cassidy was Hattie Caraway in 1944.[26][p]

Predictions

Multiple sites and political pundits have published predictions of competitive seats. These predictions have considered factors such as the strength of the incumbent (if the incumbent was running for reelection) and the other candidates, and the state's partisan lean, reflected in part by the state's Cook Partisan Voting Index rating. The predictions typically assign ratings to each seat, indicating the predicted advantage that a party had in winning that seat. Most election predictors use:

  • "tossup": no advantage
  • "tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean"
  • "lean": slight advantage
  • "likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage
  • "safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory

Race summary

Special elections during the preceding Congress

Special U.S. Senate elections in Florida and Ohio were scheduled for November 3, 2026. Florida voters reelected DeSantis appointee Ashley Moody to serve the remaining two years of former Senator Marco Rubio's unexpired term;[51] Rubio resigned his seat in 2025 to become United States Secretary of State.[52] Ohio voters elected former Senator Sherrod Brown to serve the remaining two years of former Senator JD Vance's unexpired term; Vance resigned in 2025 to become Vice President of the United States.[53]

Republican Tommy Tuberville, who was elected in 2020 with 60.1% of the vote, initially planned to seek reelection. But on May 27, 2025, he announced that he would instead run for governor of Alabama.[60]

Held on May 19, the Republican primary featured U.S. Representative Barry Moore,[61] former Navy SEAL Jared Hudson,[62] and state attorney general Steve Marshall.[63] Since no candidate reached 50%, a runoff was held on June 16 between the top two finishers. Moore won the runoff, becoming the Republican nominee.

In the Democratic primary, no candidate received 50%, so a runoff was held between businessman Dakarai Larriet and attorney Everett Wess.[64] Wess won the runoff with 54.6% of the vote.[65]

Main article: 2026 United States Senate election in Maine
See also: List of United States senators from Maine

Incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins was reelected with 51% of the vote to 42% for her Democratic opponent in 2020. She formally announced her reelection campaign in February 2026.[124] As the only person to submit the necessary number of signatures to appear on the primary ballot, Collins is the Republican nominee.[125]

According to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, as of October 2026, Collins has received $4,525,846 from political action committees (PACs) affiliated with pro-Israel lobbies; of this amount, $3,670,038 is attributed to the 2026 election cycle.[126]

Throughout 2025, Governor Janet Mills was seen as a potential Democratic challenger to Collins. She announced her Senate candidacy in October,[127] and pledged to serve only one term if elected.[128] She suspended her campaign on April 30, 2026, due to a lack of financial resources and poor polling numbers.[129]

On June 9, Sullivan harbor master and Marine veteran Graham Platner[130] defeated former deputy secretary of the Maryland Department of the Environment David Costello[131] for the Democratic nomination with 72% of the vote.[132]

On July 8, Platner announced his withdrawal from the race, following allegations of sexual assault, which he denied. The same day, Maine Democrats voted to hold a state convention to select a replacement nominee.[133] Candidates seeking the nomination were required to collect at least 500 signatures, including 50 from each of eight counties.[134] During county meetings to select convention delegates, approximately 456 delegates pledged their support to former state Senator Troy Jackson.[135][136][137] Jackson subsequently defeated Saundra Pelletier at the convention by a vote of 566–5.[138]

Two-term Republican Ben Sasse resigned early in the 118th Congress to become president of the University of Florida.[164] On January 12, 2023, Governor Jim Pillen appointed former governor Pete Ricketts as senator.[165] Ricketts won the 2024 special election to complete Sasse's term, defeating college professor Preston Love Jr.,[166] and is now running for reelection to his first full term.[167]

Former labor union leader Dan Osborn, who challenged Republican Deb Fischer for Nebraska's Class I Senate seat, has announced an independent bid.[168]

The Nebraska Democratic Party has declined to recruit a Democratic challenger to Ricketts,[169] and the party's chair has endorsed Osborn.[170] Other candidates filed for the Democratic primary, raising concern that their campaigns could split the vote and weaken Osborn's support in the general election,[171] but when retired pharmacy technician Cindy Burbank won the Democratic primary, she announced that she intended to withdraw from the general election if she saw no clear path to victory.[172] She officially withdrew from the race on July 17.[173]

Three-term Democrat Jeanne Shaheen was reelected in 2020 with 56.6% of the vote. On March 12, 2025, Shaheen announced that she would not seek reelection to a fourth term.[23]

U.S. Representative Chris Pappas[174] defeated New Hampshire Democratic Party rules committee member Karishma Manzur[175] to win the Democratic nomination on September 8.[176]

Former U.S. Senator John E. Sununu won the Republican nomination on September 8, defeating former Massachusetts U.S. Senator and U.S. Ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa Scott Brown.[176][177] Both have previously lost Senate races to Shaheen: Sununu in 2008 and Brown in 2014.[178] Sununu's brother, former Governor Chris Sununu, declined to run.[179]

Two-term Republican Thom Tillis, who was narrowly reelected in 2020 with 48.7% of the vote, announced on June 29, 2025, that he would not seek a third term after facing backlash for voting against One Big Beautiful Bill Act, prompting Donald Trump to call for a primary challenger.[59] After Tillis withdrew, Trump endorsed former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley,[187] who won the Republican nomination, defeating Don Brown in the March 3 primary.[188]

Former co-chair of the Republican National Committee Lara Trump, Donald Trump's daughter-in-law and a Wilmington native, was considered a potential candidate to challenge Tillis, but announced she would not run.[189]

On the Democratic side, former U.S. Representative Wiley Nickel declared his candidacy in April 2025.[190] Former Governor Roy Cooper entered the race on July 28, 2025.[191] Nickel withdrew the following day and endorsed Cooper,[192] who later won the Democratic nomination.[193]

One-term Republican JD Vance was elected in 2022 with 53% of the vote.[194] On January 10, 2025, he resigned from the Senate after being elected Vice President of the United States in 2024. On January 17, Governor Mike DeWine announced that then-Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted would replace Vance in the Senate.[195] Husted is running to serve the remainder of Vance's term.[196]

Former U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown, who was unseated in 2024,[197] defeated IT professional Ron Kincaid in the Democratic primary on May 5, 2026.[198]

Former Libertarian National Committee chair William Redpath is running as a Libertarian.[199] Ohio Libertarians disqualified healthcare consultant Jeffrey Kanter from the Libertarian primary after he submitted hundreds of invalid signatures with his candidate petition.[200]

Main article: 2026 United States Senate election in Oklahoma
See also: List of United States senators from Oklahoma

Incumbent Republican Markwayne Mullin won a special election in 2022 with 61.8% of the vote to complete the remainder of the term vacated by Jim Inhofe, who resigned on January 3, 2023, due to declining health and died in 2024.[201]

Mullin initially announced plans to seek his first full term in office, but on March 5, 2026, President Trump announced his nomination of Mullin for Secretary of Homeland Security; the Senate confirmed Mullin on March 23.[202] Governor Kevin Stitt appointed board member and former CEO of Williams Companies Alan Armstrong to replace Mullin in the Senate.[203] Armstrong was sworn in on March 24[204] and was required to sign an oath stating that he would not run in the 2026 election.[205][14]

U.S. Representative for Oklahoma's 1st congressional district Kevin Hern[206] won the June 16 Republican primary with 70% of the vote in a crowded field.[207]

In the June 16 Democratic primary, mediator Jim Priest[208] and nurse N'Kiyla "Jasmine" Thomas[209] received the most votes and advanced to an August 25 runoff.[210] Thomas, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, won the runoff with 61% of the vote.

Entering Wedge Media executive director Ron Meinhardt and pharmacist Curtis Stinnett are running as independents.[207][211] Sevier White, candidate for Oklahoma's 4th congressional district in 2016, is running as a Libertarian.[207]

Four-term Republican Lindsey Graham was reelected in 2020 with 54.4% of the vote and was seeking a fifth term.[221] He won the June 9 Republican primary with 57% of the vote,[222] but died in office on July 11.[223] Governor Henry McMaster appointed Lindsey Graham's sister, Darline Graham, to serve the remainder of his term. She subsequently sought a full term. In the August 11 special Republican primary, Darline Graham and U.S. Representative Ralph Norman advanced to an August 25 runoff, which Graham won with 52% of the vote to Norman's 48%.[224]

Pediatrician Annie Andrews[225] won the Democratic primary with 61% of the vote.[226]

The South Carolina Libertarian Party nominee was Kasie Whitener, a novelist, business consultant, radio host and Clinical Assistant Professor of Entrepreneurship at the University of South Carolina.[227] The Constitution Party nominee was Mark Hackett, a house painter. Both candidates were nominated by their respective party conventions.[228] 2022 US Senate candidate Catherine Fleming Bruce ran as a write-in candidate.

Main article: 2026 United States Senate election in Texas
See also: List of United States senators from Texas

Four-term Republican John Cornyn was reelected in 2020 with 53.5% of the vote, and ran for a fifth term in 2026.[237]

Cornyn and state Attorney General Ken Paxton ran in the Republican primary on March 3. Since neither received more than 50% of the vote, they advanced to a runoff election held on May 26.[238] U.S. Representative for the 38th congressional district Wesley Hunt challenged Paxton and Cornyn, but lost the primary.[239] On May 19, both Hunt and President Trump endorsed Paxton.[240] Paxton defeated Cornyn in the runoff by a landslide and became the Republican nominee.

State Representative James Talarico is the Democratic nominee, having defeated U.S. Representative Jasmine Crockett in the primary.[241][242] Talarico defeated Paxton by 12.1 points, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988.
